canonical_topic: Illustrative example: an irrational end-of-day trade forcing a market-wide markdown
definition: A hypothetical scenario where a trader, wanting to finish a large sale before a holiday weekend and running low on willing buyers, accepts a much lower price on the last block of a transaction late in the trading day; because it is the final reported trade, it becomes the mark used by everyone holding that asset.
core_idea: A single trader's non-distressed, time-pressured decision can become the price that forces a substantial paper loss across all holders of the asset, even though the broader market was functioning normally.
key_points: The trader sells the final portion of a large position at a discount near market close to avoid trading during a vacation.
Because it lands at end of day, this trade is likely to be the last reported price for the asset.
Everyone holding the asset must then mark their books to this final, discounted price.
The author notes the trade wasn't evidence of market distress -- it was a normal transaction between willing counterparties, just one that didn't maximize the seller's profit.
relationships: Illustrates the systemic-risk problem of thin trading volume setting the mark
trading_implications: End-of-day or pre-holiday illiquidity can let a single trade set a mark that misrepresents the broader market's equilibrium price.
Holders of an asset can suffer a mark-to-market loss driven by one counterparty's scheduling convenience rather than by fundamental repricing.
caveats: Interpreting a large, off-market final trade as a sign of genuine market distress rather than an idiosyncratic, liquidity-driven event.
